Brants (Parotomys brantsii), a social rodent inhabiting the arid shrublands of southern Africa, exhibits a life history finely tuned to an unpredictable environment. Back-extrapolation of growth trajectories from longitudinal field data places the wet weight at birth at approximately 12 grams [Wwb = approximately 12 grams], a modest neonatal mass that reflects the relatively short gestation period of this murid rodent. At a core body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], gestation has been recorded to last 38 days [tg = 38 days], a duration that is typical for small-bodied, semi-precocial rodents. This abbreviated intrauterine phase allows females to compress the reproductive cycle, a strategy often linked to exploiting brief pulses of primary productivity following sporadic rainfall events in the Karoo. Litter sizes typically range from 3 to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 to 4 pups per litter], and females produce approximately 3 to 4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 to 4 litters per year] under favorable conditions.

Lactation represents a substantial energetic drain for female Brants, yet weaning is a comparatively rapid process when considered within the broader context of otomyine life histories. At the same regulated body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 40 days [tx = 40 days], after which the young must transition to an independent, herbivorous diet. By this stage, the wet weight at weaning is roughly 80 grams [Wwx = roughly 80 grams], a figure that represents a nearly seven-fold increase over the neonatal mass. This steep pre-weaning growth trajectory is sustained entirely through maternal milk provisioning and is consistent with the pattern observed in other gregarious African murids that occupy open, seasonal environments. Weaning synchrony across the litter likely facilitates the early dispersal or integration of juveniles into the colony's complex social structure, where alloparental care and burrow sharing are common.

Sexual maturation in Brants proceeds more slowly than the rapid pre-weaning gains might suggest. At 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 70 days [tp = 70 days], marking the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to contribute to the colony's reproductive output. This developmental delay, relative to the weaning date, likely reflects the need for juveniles to achieve a threshold body condition and fat reserve before investing in gametogenesis. The ultimate wet weight, or the asymptotic adult body mass, is approximately 129.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 129.5 grams], indicating that significant somatic growth continues well after reproductive maturity is attained. This pattern of asymptotic mass being reached considerably after puberty aligns with a life history strategy where early reproduction is not foregone but the full size potential is realized gradually through an extended sub-adult period.

The maximum lifespan of Parotomys brantsii, as documented from mark-recapture studies and confirmed by captive records, reaches 5 years [am = 5 years] under the species' typical thermoneutral conditions of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. This longevity is notably extended for a rodent of its body size, exceeding the typical lifespan of many similarly sized murids by a factor of two or more and suggesting a relatively slow pace of life. The maximum reproductive rate, realized as a combination of litter size and event frequency, can be expressed as females producing a single litter approximately every breeding season [F_R_i = a single litter approximately every breeding season], containing 3 to 4 pups [N_R_i = containing 3 to 4 pups], with the potential for multiple litters per year if conditions remain favorable. The survival advantage conferred by the species' elaborate burrow systems, providing thermal buffering and predation refuge, is a probable contributor to this extended longevity.

Populations of Brants occupying the Nama-Karoo, where ambient temperatures can fluctuate dramatically between seasons, typically achieve the developmental milestones described above when their core body temperature is maintained at 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. The time since birth at weaning, recorded as 40 days [tx = 40 days], coupled with the wet weight at weaning of 80 grams [Wwx = 80 grams], provides a critical benchmark for assessing nutritional stress in wild colonies at a temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. Field observations confirm that adult female body mass plateaus at the ultimate wet weight of 129.5 grams [Wwi = 129.5 grams], although some gravid individuals may briefly exceed this figure during late gestation when the combined mass of developing pups and maternal tissues peaks. Comparative life table analyses across colonies reveal that the maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] is attained only in well-established warrens with stable food resources, while isolated or marginal populations rarely exceed three years at a temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. The reproductive performance under these thermoneutral conditions underscores the species' capacity for rapid population increase during favorable windows.
